Acoustic metamaterials and simulating topological insulators

What does the content of the previous two articles (When acoustics meets condensed matter, part 1 and part 2) have to do with acoustics? This is where one of the hottest topics in acoustics, and in physical acoustics especially, comes in: acoustic metamaterials. In short, acoustic metamaterials have deliberately engineered structures that control and modulate sound waves passing through them in a targeted way, yielding effective macroscopic material parameters (such as a negative elastic modulus or a negative refractive index) or wave-control effects that are hard to achieve with conventional materials. For example, Prof. Ping Sheng of the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) and colleagues have used acoustic resonators to design structures that confine a material’s absorption to a specific frequency band [2]; in 2009, Prof. Jianchun Cheng of Nanjing University and colleagues designed an acoustic diode that rectifies sound waves much as a diode rectifies electric current [3]; and so on. Metamaterials also play a part in other areas, such as acoustic focusing, acoustic imaging and acoustic tweezers. This article looks at a relatively new application of metamaterials: simulating condensed matter phenomena, mainly in topological materials.

The principle is actually quite simple. The time-independent Schrödinger equation obeyed by the electron wave function in a material and the wave equation obeyed by sound waves are both second-order linear partial differential equations, so mathematically the two really are alike. And since we can calculate the band structure of electrons in a periodic potential, we can define something similar for sound waves. In that case, the role of the “periodic potential” is played by a purpose-designed metamaterial.

Take a 2015 paper by Zhaoju Yang et al. [1] as an example. The authors designed a periodic structure, shown in Figure 8. Gray cylinders are arranged periodically on a triangular lattice. Each cylinder is immersed in a layer of fluid of a given width, and the cylinder and its surrounding fluid are in turn immersed in, but separated from, the outer fluid. The cylinders rotate at a set angular velocity and, through the fluid’s viscosity, set the fluid around them rotating too.

Figure 8. Schematic of a two-dimensional acoustic topological insulator [1]

The wave equation governing sound propagation in this structure can be written in a form that looks very much like the time-independent Schrödinger equation with an electromagnetic potential:

And the energy spectrum that comes out of the calculation closely resembles that of the real topological insulators discussed earlier:

Figure 9. Band structure of the acoustic topological insulator [1]

The figure below shows the calculated sound pressure distribution of an acoustic edge state propagating along the boundary. Notice that the sound travels in one direction only along the edge and decays toward the interior, exactly as an edge state should.

Figure 10. Band structure of the acoustic topological insulator [1]

That work was purely computational. The first real experimental realization came in 2019, from Prof. Jianchun Cheng’s group at Nanjing University. The structure they designed resembles the theoretical one above, as shown below. Each lattice site consists of a rotating disk driven by a motor, and the disks are connected by waveguides, so the whole structure follows the tight-binding model of a crystal. Sound is fed in at one point and propagates from there.

Figure 11. Schematic of the experimental acoustic topological insulator [4]

The experimental results, shown below, also look very much like the band structure of a real topological insulator. The red and blue lines are the upper and lower edge states. In Figure 13, the left and right panels show the measured sound pressure of the upper and lower edge states, and the middle panel shows a topologically trivial bulk state.

Figure 12. Schematic of the experimental acoustic topological insulator [4]

Figure 13. Measured sound pressure of the edge states [4]

In fact, such simulations are not limited to topological insulators. Just about every well-known structure in condensed matter physics has probably been tried by now: Weyl semimetals, Majorana zero modes and more, which I won’t go into here. Because these metamaterials modulate sound through their periodicity, they are sometimes also called phononic crystals. Seen this way, the name is rather apt.

About the author: jemand has a bachelor’s degree in physics from Nanjing University, is studying for a master’s in physics at RWTH Aachen University, and will probably end up working in acoustics. That’s all.

References

[1] Z. Yang, F. Gao, X. Shi, X. Lin, Z. Gao, Y. Chong, and B. Zhang, Phys. Rev. Lett. 114, 114301 (2015).

[2] M. Yang, S. Chen, C. Fu, and P. Sheng, Materials Horizons, 4(4), 673–680 (2017).

[3] B. Liang, B. Yuan, and J. Cheng, Phys. Rev. Lett. 103, 104301 (2009).

[4] Y. Ding, Y. Peng, Y. Zhu, X. Fan, J. Yang, B. Liang, X. Zhu, X. Wan, and J. Cheng, Phys. Rev. Lett. 122, 014302 (2019).
